definition: Neurorobotics is the combined study of neuroscience, robotics, and artificial intelligence.
details: It is the science and technology of embodied autonomous neural systems. Neural systems include brain-inspired algorithms (e.g. connectionist networks), computational models of biological neural networks (e.g. artificial spiking neural networks, large-scale simulations of neural microcircuits) and actual biological systems (e.g. in vivo and in vitro neural nets). Such neural systems can be embodied in machines with mechanic or any other forms of physical actuation. This includes robots, prosthetic or wearable systems but also, at smaller scale, micro-machines and, at the larger scales, furniture and infrastructures. Neurorobotics is that branch of neuroscience with robotics, which deals with the study and application of science and technology of embodied autonomous neural systems like brain-inspired algorithms. It is based on the idea that the brain is embodied and the body is embedded in the environment. Therefore, most neurorobots are required to function in the real world, as opposed to a simulated environment. Beyond brain-inspired algorithms for robots neurorobotics may also involve the design of brain-controlled robot systems.

explainer.lead: Neurorobotics combines neuroscience, robotics, and AI to study embodied autonomous neural systems. It matters because it tests brain-inspired algorithms in bodies that must act in the physical world, not just on data.

tiers.eli5: Instead of testing a model of a brain only on a screen, you give it a body and see whether it can cope with the real world.
tiers.practitioner: Practitioners embody connectionist networks, spiking network models, or even biological neural nets in machines with mechanical or other physical actuation; a pitfall is treating simulated microcircuits as equivalent to the biological systems they mimic.
tiers.paperLevel: Neurorobotics is the science and technology of embodied autonomous neural systems, where neural systems span brain-inspired algorithms, computational models of biological neural networks such as artificial spiking networks and large-scale microcircuit simulations, and actual biological systems such as in vivo and in vitro neural nets, embodied in machines with mechanical or other physical actuation.

explainer.example: A simulated spiking neural network controls a robotic limb, letting researchers observe how its dynamics behave under real actuation.
